items.stem: A clinician tells a patient that a shoulder joint is like the skull sutures because all joints are structurally identical. What correction is most accurate?
options: All joints are identical, so mobility depends only on muscles.
Synovial joints have a joint cavity and specialized structures.
Every joint lacks ligaments and cartilage.
A joint cavity means the joint cannot move.
items.explanation: Synovial joints are not structurally identical to all other joints. Their joint cavity, articular cartilage, synovial fluid, and ligaments support smooth motion and resist abnormal motion.
items.familyKey: students may treat every joint as structurally identical

items.stem: An amateur astronomer buys a larger telescope hoping to make dim galaxies brighter, but the view is only bigger, not clearer. What should they understand?
options: Magnification is the telescope's main purpose.
Light-gathering area matters; doubling aperture quadruples light.
A smaller aperture always resolves more detail.
Magnification alone reveals fainter objects.
items.explanation: Telescope performance depends on light-gathering area, not just magnification. Doubling aperture quadruples collected light, while magnification alone can only enlarge a dim blur.
items.familyKey: students think a telescope s main purpose is magnification

items.stem: A nearby star shows a much larger annual shift against background stars than another star. What does that imply?
options: It is more distant, because larger parallax means farther away.
It is nearer, because parallax shrinks with distance.
Its parsec value must be zero.
Its motion is unrelated to distance.
items.explanation: Parallax and distance are inverse. Nearby stars shift the most, and a star twice as far shows half the parallax.
items.familyKey: students expect a larger parallax to mean a more distant sta

items.stem: A student wonders why Mercury and Venus are rocky while Jupiter and Saturn contain much more ice and gas. Which explanation best fits the solar nebula hypothesis?
options: The arrangement is coincidence from random planet collisions.
The disk temperature gradient determined what could condense.
All planets formed from identical amounts of rock.
Outer planets are only large because they are older.
items.explanation: The temperature gradient of the disk explains the architecture. Near the hot Sun, only metals and rock condensed; beyond the frost line, ices condensed too, providing more building material.
items.familyKey: students treat the arrangement of rocky inner planets and ic

items.stem: During exercise, a runner's body temperature rises, then sweating cools it back toward normal. Which statement best describes homeostasis?
options: The body keeps temperature completely unchanging.
Homeostasis is active regulation around a set point.
Homeostasis means the body stops responding.
Sweating proves the set point does not matter.
items.explanation: Homeostasis is active regulation around a set point, not a frozen constant. Negative feedback counters the change and returns the variable toward the set point.
items.familyKey: students think homeostasis means an unchanging internal stat

items.stem: In lab, a group titrates an acid sample using a titrant they never standardized, yet they still record an endpoint and calculate concentration. What is the main flaw?
options: The endpoint is meaningful without knowing titrant concentration.
The titrant must be standardized before the endpoint matters.
Standardization only applies after the endpoint.
Endpoint readings replace concentration measurements.
items.explanation: The endpoint is only meaningful once the titrant's concentration is known. Titration steps are sequential, and an unstandardized titrant makes the result invalid.
items.familyKey: students read an endpoint from a titrant that was never stan

items.stem: A central bank sees prices and wages keep rising after each increase. What best describes this cycle?
options: Positive feedback amplifies the initial change.
Negative feedback restores stability.
Positive feedback always produces good outcomes.
Wage-price spiral means prices stop changing.
items.explanation: Positive feedback describes runaway amplification, not automatic benefit. In an inflation spiral, rising prices lead to higher wages and then still higher prices.
items.familyKey: students assume positive feedback is beneficial when it name

items.conceptName: Radical Republicans and the Wade–Davis Bill
items.stem: A Reconstruction plan requires the Ironclad Oath from many former Confederates and excludes many from politics. Compared with Lincoln’s approach, how was it viewed?
options: It was more lenient than Lincoln's plan.
It was harsher than Lincoln's plan.
It matched Lincoln's plan exactly.
It ended Reconstruction immediately.
items.explanation: The Wade–Davis Bill was harsher, requiring the Ironclad Oath and excluding many from political participation. Lincoln blocked it with a pocket veto.
items.familyKey: the wade davis bill was more lenient than lincoln s plan

items.stem: A textbook asks when the Thirteenth Amendment legally ended slavery in the United States. Which statement is correct?
options: It was ratified during Lincoln's lifetime.
It ended slavery only in the North.
It was ratified after Lincoln died.
It replaced the Emancipation Proclamation.
items.explanation: Lincoln never saw the final ratification of the Thirteenth Amendment. The amendment permanently abolished slavery after his death.
items.familyKey: the thirteenth amendment was ratified during lincoln s lifet

items.conceptName: Overland migration trails (Oregon Trail and others)
items.stem: A family in 1852 joins a wagon train on the Oregon Trail. Why does the journey remain risky even with many travelers?
options: Large groups guaranteed safety.
Illness and starvation were still common.
Native people always attacked wagon trains.
The route was only a few hundred miles.
items.explanation: The trails were dangerous even for large groups. Illness, starvation, and other hazards made survival difficult on long wagon journeys.
items.familyKey: wagon trains were typically safe because large numbers guara

items.conceptName: Drivers of late nineteenth-century U.S. urbanization
items.stem: A city’s population surges in the 1880s as factories add electric lights and immigrants arrive near ports. What best explains the growth?
options: Urban growth was already explosive in colonial times.
Industrialization and new technology drew people into cities.
Factories moved back to farms near rivers.
Cities grew only because of wagon trains.
items.explanation: The explosion in urban population growth came later, in the mid-nineteenth century. Industrialization, new technologies, and immigration concentrated jobs and people in cities.
items.familyKey: urban population growth in the u s was already explosive fro

items.stem: A downtown developer wants to build a 20-story office tower in 1890. Which invention makes that height practical for daily use?
options: Steel frame construction alone
The electric elevator
The telegraph
The electric trolley
items.explanation: Steel helped, but tall buildings needed another vital invention: the elevator. The first electric elevator in 1889 made skyscrapers usable, not just possible.
items.familyKey: skyscrapers became common as soon as steel construction exis

items.conceptName: The Grange, Granger Laws, and the Greenback Party
items.stem: Midwestern farmers form cooperatives to buy supplies together and demand fair railroad rates. Which belief best fits the Grange's strategy?
options: Violent confrontation with railroads
Self-help through cooperatives
Ending all currency use
Joining city factory unions
items.explanation: The Grange emphasized self-help through cooperatives to pool resources and negotiate better rates. It pursued organization and regulation, not violence against railroads or banks.
items.familyKey: the grange mainly sought violent confrontation with railroad

items.conceptName: African American soldiers (“Smoked Yankees”) in the Spanish-American War
items.stem: In a Black community meeting, some residents urge enlistment while others warn the war will deepen inequality. What view matches the historical debate?
options: All Black Americans supported the war
There was debate for and against involvement
Black soldiers were kept entirely from service
The war had no connection to citizenship
items.explanation: Black Americans did not respond uniformly; the passage describes debate both for and against involvement. Those views reflected different ideas about citizenship, obligation, and opportunity.
items.familyKey: black americans uniformly supported participation in the war

items.stem: During a debate, a student says Wilson backed intervention abroad only because it protected U.S. business and power, not because of any higher principle. Which interpretation best fits the text?
options: Wilson was purely self-interested, not moral.
Wilson framed intervention as a moral imperative.
Wilson opposed all overseas markets.
Wilson rejected diplomacy and peace talks.
items.explanation: The text describes Wilson’s idealistic foreign policy as grounded in morality and a moral imperative, even if practice diverged. It also notes he still valued U.S. values and overseas markets, so “purely self-interest” is too narrow.
items.familyKey: wilson s foreign policy was purely about u s self interest n

items.conceptName: European alliance system at the outbreak of World War I
items.stem: At the start of World War I, a student says the Triple Alliance and Triple Entente were simply the same as the later Central and Allied powers. What is the best correction?
options: They were identical from the start.
They became opposing sides after war began.
Italy never changed sides.
Austria-Hungary joined the Entente.
items.explanation: The prewar alliance system transformed after the outbreak of war into opposing camps. The text emphasizes the Triple Entente and Triple Alliance first, then the Central Powers and Allied Powers later, with Italy’s neutrality and switch showing the change.
items.familyKey: the triple alliance and triple entente were the same thing a

items.conceptName: Emergency Banking Act of 1933 (bank holiday and reform)
items.stem: After the 1933 bank holiday, a student says people could still exchange dollar bills for gold exactly as before. What does the text say instead?
options: Gold redemption continued unchanged.
Dollar bills were no longer redeemable in gold.
Only banks could redeem gold.
Gold became the only legal currency.
items.explanation: The Emergency Banking Act ended redemption of dollar bills in gold and took the country off the gold standard. The law expanded federal control, so the old convertibility was not preserved.
items.familyKey: going off the gold standard meant people could still redeem

items.stem: In a county facing mass unemployment, a New Deal administrator argues for federal aid. Which response best matches the work relief programs described in the passage?
options: Send cash handouts to unemployed families.
Use grants and public jobs to employ workers.
Wait for private industry to recover.
Expand tariffs to protect wages.
items.explanation: FERA and the CWA emphasized grants, relief agencies, and public employment, not just cash handouts. The passage says Roosevelt mostly wanted to create more jobs through mass employment on projects like roads and bridges.
items.familyKey: new deal relief was mainly cash handouts rather than jobs

items.stem: A textbook chapter on the Munich Pact includes maps of the Sudetenland and Czechoslovakia. What is the pact mainly about?
options: Reducing navies through disarmament.
Territorial concessions to Germany.
Creating a Soviet-German alliance.
Ending trade barriers in Europe.
items.explanation: The Munich Pact concerned territorial concessions in Czechoslovakia, especially German occupation of the Sudetenland. It was not mainly about arms limits or naval reductions.
items.familyKey: the munich pact was mainly about reducing navies or arms lim

items.stem: After World War II, a student says the Cold War was only about Europe because the U.S. and USSR fought mainly over Berlin and Germany. Which response best corrects this view?
options: Only Europe mattered; Asia was unrelated.
It also involved poorer nations and wars like Korea and Vietnam.
It was a direct war between U.S. and Soviet troops.
It ended immediately in 1945.
items.explanation: The Cold War was not limited to Europe. Its influence extended to poorer nations and conflicts such as Korea and Vietnam, showing a broad global struggle for influence, not just a European dispute.
items.familyKey: only europe mattered in the cold war

items.stem: A classmate claims containment meant the United States should immediately overthrow Communist governments wherever they appeared. Which statement best fits Kennan’s strategy?
options: Overthrow Communist governments everywhere at once.
Limit Soviet influence where it already existed.
Stay out of all foreign conflicts.
Support Soviet expansion into new regions.
items.explanation: Containment aimed to limit Soviet influence to those places where it already existed. It was meant to prevent expansion into new areas, not launch immediate regime change everywhere.
items.familyKey: containment meant immediately overthrowing communist governm

items.stem: A student says containment was mostly a domestic campaign against American Communists at home. Which interpretation matches the text?
options: A domestic anti-Communist purge.
A foreign policy to restrict Soviet influence abroad.
A plan to end all elections.
A program to nationalize U.S. industry.
items.explanation: In this section, containment is a foreign policy strategy. It restricts Soviet influence abroad and includes economic policy and security reorganization, not mainly domestic policing.
items.familyKey: containment was mainly a domestic anti communist policy

items.stem: A student argues the Marshall Plan was only charity for starving Europeans and had no U.S. interests. What best corrects that claim?
options: It was purely humanitarian aid only.
It had economic and political goals too.
It was meant to punish Britain.
It funded only military bases.
items.explanation: The plan was not purely humanitarian. Truman’s motivation was economic and political, as well as humanitarian, and requiring purchases of American goods boosted U.S. economy and cultural presence.
items.familyKey: the marshall plan was purely humanitarian and had no politic

items.conceptName: Brown v. Board of Education (1954) holding
items.stem: A classmate says Brown v. Board immediately integrated most Southern schools in 1954. Which detail best corrects that claim?
options: Integration happened slowly under deliberate speed.
Most schools integrated by 1955.
Segregation increased after Brown.
Only Northern schools were affected.
items.explanation: Brown did not produce immediate large-scale integration. The Court ordered desegregation with all deliberate speed, and by 1960 fewer than 10 percent of Southern Black students attended integrated schools.
items.familyKey: brown immediately integrated southern schools at large scale

items.stem: A student describes the Reagan Revolution as just Reagan’s upbeat speaking style. What is the better explanation?
options: Only a communication style, not policy.
A conservative agenda and voter coalition.
A return to New Deal liberalism.
A movement against elections.
items.explanation: The Reagan Revolution refers to a conservative political turn, not just personality. It involved a voter coalition and policy priorities that reshaped later U.S. politics.
items.familyKey: the reagan revolution describes only reagan s personality an

items.stem: After Reagan fires striking PATCO controllers, a commentator says he was still flexible toward unions while deregulating industry. What best fits the text?
options: Correct; he remained flexible toward unions.
Wrong; he was less flexible and weakened labor unions.
Correct; PATCO strengthened union bargaining power.
Wrong; deregulation increased union influence.
items.explanation: The passage says Reagan was “less flexible” about deregulation and “weakening the power of labor unions.” Firing PATCO helped destroy the union and signaled an employer shift toward replacing striking workers.
items.familyKey: reagan was consistently flexible toward unions even while de

items.stem: A classmate argues the Bush Doctrine was only a plan for invading Afghanistan after 9/11. What is the best correction?
options: It was only about Afghanistan and one battle.
It described pre-emptive war and regime change broadly.
It rejected self-protection against terrorism.
It applied only to NATO allies.
items.explanation: The definition presents the Bush Doctrine as a general policy about U.S. rights and tools, including pre-emption and regime change. It was not limited to Afghanistan; it framed a broader war on terrorism.
items.familyKey: the bush doctrine was only about afghanistan and had nothing

items.stem: A Korean learner wants to say “three apples,” “three years old,” and “three o’clock” on the same worksheet. Which choice best fits all three uses?
options: Use one number system everywhere.
Use the context-appropriate number system and counters.
Always use native Korean without counters.
Always translate directly from English.
items.explanation: Different contexts favor different number systems. Age, quantity, and time all require the grammatical setting to guide whether native Korean or Sino-Korean forms, plus counters, are needed.
items.familyKey: one korean number system is used for every counting situatio

items.stem: A student writes the sentence as “Teacher book read” and leaves out all particles. What is the best revision strategy?
options: Particles are optional decoration.
Keep the word order and ignore endings.
Use particles to show each noun’s role.
Drop the verb because it is already implied.
items.explanation: Particles carry grammatical meaning and help show what each noun is doing in the sentence. In Korean, they matter for interpretation, along with verb-final order and a final ending.
items.familyKey: particles are optional decoration

items.stem: At a job interview in Korean, a speaker uses plain endings and informal vocabulary with the interviewer. What is the most accurate concern?
options: Politeness is optional and does not affect grammar.
Only pronunciation matters in this situation.
Politeness shapes endings and word choice.
Honorifics are used only in writing.
items.explanation: Politeness is built into Korean grammar and strongly shapes how sentences are formed. The situation and social relationship affect sentence endings and vocabulary, so plain speech can sound inappropriate.
items.familyKey: politeness is optional and does not affect grammar

items.stem: While drafting about a novel, a student lists symbols, colors, and names but never explains how they support a claim about the book’s meaning. What should the student do?
options: Catalogue more details without interpretation.
Require each detail to support the whole work.
Ignore the whole and focus on one line.
Replace analysis with summary.
items.explanation: Require each detail to earn its place by supporting an interpretive claim about the whole. Close reading moves between part and whole, so description alone is not enough.
items.familyKey: students catalogue textual details without connecting them t

items.stem: A writer submits a 20-line love poem with no refrain and irregular line lengths, calling it a ghazal. What is the best response?
options: A ghazal is just any poem about love and separation.
It needs couplets, equal line lengths, and a refrain.
It must be written only in Arabic.
It must have exactly one speaker and one stanza.
items.explanation: Topic alone is not enough. A ghazal uses couplets with a repeating rhyme+refrain scheme and equal line lengths, so the form requires more than love and separation.
items.familyKey: a ghazal is just any poem about love and separation

items.conceptName: Metrical feet and metrical line length
items.stem: An assignment asks for iambic pentameter, and a student writes a five-syllable line. What is the main problem?
options: Pentameter means five syllables.
Pentameter is five feet, not five syllables.
Iambs cannot be used in English.
The line must have ten stresses.
items.explanation: Pentameter is defined here as a five-foot line, not five syllables. The pattern concerns metrical feet, such as iambs, rather than counting syllables alone.
items.familyKey: pentameter means a line has five syllables

items.stem: A student says, “When I read the poem, the five senses are just metaphorical; they are not real ways I process the text.” Which response best fits the passage’s view of poetry?
options: Senses are natural powers that receive information from words.
Senses are metaphorical decorations, not cognitive inputs.
Poetry avoids sensory experience and favors abstraction.
Reading only involves logic, not mental images.
items.explanation: The passage treats senses as natural powers for receiving information, and says reading turns words into mental images involving the five senses. It rejects the idea that we understand mainly through abstract thought alone.
items.familyKey: the senses in reading are metaphorical rather than real cogn

items.conceptName: Genre purpose and density of imagery
items.stem: A writer says her diary is meant to shape public opinion, so she fills it with persuasive images. Which choice best matches the section?
options: A diary is usually private and not aimed at outsiders.
A diary is mainly written to affect an outside audience.
A diary should use more images than a poem.
A diary is identical to a news article.
items.explanation: The section describes a diary as usually private, with little attention to affecting an outside audience. That fits the genre contrast: literary forms are image-rich, while private or utilitarian forms are not.
items.familyKey: a diary entry is written primarily to affect an outside audi

items.stem: After one quick read, a student says, “I already figured out the poem’s meaning, so there’s no need to read it again.” What is the best advice?
options: Figure out the meaning as quickly as possible.
Use total response and reread attentively.
Ignore emotion and focus on paraphrase.
Skip listening and rely on assumptions.
items.explanation: Total response emphasizes attentive listening, nonjudgment, and rereading so emotional meanings can emerge over time. The poem is not reduced to a quick paraphrase; readers return to its words, lines, and music.
items.familyKey: reading a poem well mainly means figuring out what it means

items.stem: During discussion, a student keeps saying, “First I need to judge whether I agree with the speaker.” What reading stance is the passage recommending instead?
options: Set aside ego and imagine the speaker’s perspective.
Center your own opinions before listening.
Interrupt to correct the speaker’s view.
Treat the speaker as irrelevant to meaning.
items.explanation: Negative capability asks the reader to set aside ego and imagine the speaker’s perspective. The goal is nonjudgmental listening, as if the poem’s universe is the only one that exists.
items.familyKey: to read a poem well you should focus on your own opinions fi

items.stem: Before reading a poem called “Winter Hospital,” a student ignores the title and starts at line one. What does close reading recommend?
options: Treat the title as a doorway into the poem.
Assume the title has no interpretive value.
Wait until the end to consider the title.
Use the title only as a label.
items.explanation: Close reading begins at the title because it sets expectations for mood, tone, setting, or time. The title is a doorway that prepares the reader for what follows.
items.familyKey: the title is just a label and doesn t affect interpretation

items.stem: A teacher points to mismatched armor, burial customs, and dialects in the Iliad. A student says these flaws show the poem was badly written. What does the passage suggest instead?
options: They prove the poem is poorly made.
They are expected results of composite formation.
They show a later translator made mistakes.
They are irrelevant because the poem is fiction.
items.explanation: The passage treats mixed dialects and inconsistent details as artifacts of long composite formation. Oral transmission across time can preserve a traditional story while leaving uneven details.
items.familyKey: inconsistencies in armor burial practices or language prove

items.conceptName: Odyssey vs. Iliad: thematic focus and heroism
items.stem: A student claims the Odyssey is mainly the next chapter of the Trojan War story. Which interpretation best matches the passage?
options: It continues the war in a direct sequel.
It is only loosely connected to the Iliad.
It retells the Iliad from Helen’s view.
It rejects all Homeric heroism.
items.explanation: The passage says the Odyssey continues the Iliad only in “the loosest sense.” Its heart is homecoming, family restoration, and adventure rather than the war narrative.
items.familyKey: the odyssey is mainly a sequel to the iliad that continues t

items.stem: A director wants to stage a Shakespeare scene and assumes the script already gives exact blocking, costumes, and gestures. Which interpretation fits the passage?
options: Shakespeare provides exact stage directions.
Staging must be inferred and decided.
Only modern plays need directors.
Costumes are never interpretive.
items.explanation: The passage emphasizes that Shakespeare lacks detailed stage directions. A directorial reading therefore asks the reader to infer delivery, blocking, costumes, and setting from the text.
items.familyKey: shakespeare s plays contain detailed stage directions that t

items.conceptName: Picaresque satire (the traveler as social touchstone)
items.stem: In a seminar on Don Quixote, a student claims picaresque satire mainly tracks a traveler’s feelings and private growth. What is the better interpretation?
options: It centers on inner psychological development.
It uses movement through classes for social critique.
It avoids satire and praises each setting.
It focuses only on one fixed social class.
items.explanation: Picaresque movement across classes makes each new social setting a target of satiric vision. The result is broad social critique, not mainly inward psychological development.
items.familyKey: picaresque satire focuses on a hero s inner psychological de

items.conceptName: Gender bias in literary publication and canon formation
items.stem: A professor notes that Little Women is still often treated as “for girls,” while Huckleberry Finn is assigned as universal. What issue does this illustrate?
options: Popularity ends gender bias in publishing.
Gendered assumptions shape canon formation.
Women always wrote for only female readers.
Curricula ignore all older novels equally.
items.explanation: The passage stresses enduring assumptions about “universal” male experience and curricular patterns. Popularity does not erase gender bias in publication, reception, or classroom selection.
items.familyKey: if a work is popular gender bias in reception and curricula

items.stem: A 6-by-2 matrix has two pivot columns. What can you conclude about its rank?
options: Its rank is 6 because it has six rows.
Its rank is at most 2.
Its rank equals the number of rows.
Its rank is always large for tall matrices.
items.explanation: Rank never exceeds the smaller of the row and column counts. For a 6-by-2 matrix, the most it can have is 2, and dependence among columns can lower it further.
items.familyKey: a tall matrix with many rows has large rank

items.stem: As x approaches 3, a function stays near 2 on the left and near 7 on the right. What kind of discontinuity is this?
options: Removable, because it is not defined.
Jump, because the pieces do not meet up.
Infinite, because it goes to infinity.
Continuous, because both sides exist.
items.explanation: Jump discontinuities are noninfinite. The graph’s pieces do not meet up, so this is a jump discontinuity rather than an infinite discontinuity.
items.familyKey: a jump discontinuity means the function goes to infinity

items.stem: A business analyst uses the derivative of profit to estimate how profit changes when sales increase slightly. What is the best interpretation?
options: Only a graph-slope formula.
A rate of change used in applications.
A replacement for limits.
A method for proving continuity.
items.explanation: The text connects derivatives to rates of change in physics, business, and biology. So the derivative is not just a slope formula; it is a quantity used in applications.
items.familyKey: the derivative is only a formula for slopes of graphs not a

items.stem: For f(x)=|x| at x=0, a student says the derivative must exist because the function is defined there. Is that correct?
options: Yes; defined means differentiable.
No; the limit must exist.
Yes; every point has a derivative.
No; derivatives ignore limits.
items.explanation: Both derivative definitions require the stated limit to exist. Being defined at the point is not enough, so a derivative does not automatically exist there.
items.familyKey: a derivative always exists at every point

items.stem: A student differentiates h(x)=(x^2+1)^5 as 5(x^2+1)^4 and stops there. What is missing?
options: Multiply by the derivative of x^2+1
Evaluate the outer derivative at x
Subtract 1 from the exponent
Replace 5 with 1
items.explanation: Every chain-rule derivative has two factors: f′ evaluated at g(x), then times g′(x). If no inner derivative appears, the chain rule was not applied.
items.familyKey: students differentiate the outer function and stop forgettin

items.stem: A student finds d/dx of (3x+2)^4 as 4(3x+2)^3 and then substitutes x for the outer derivative. What should the outer derivative use?
options: g(x), not x
x, not g(x)
the constant 4
the inner derivative only
items.explanation: The outer derivative is evaluated at g(x), not x: h′(x)=f′(g(x))·g′(x), never f′(x)·g′(x). The chain rule works from the outside function in.

items.stem: A relation x^2+y^2=25 is given, and y is not solved for. Which method is appropriate to find dy/dx?
options: Implicit differentiation
Only explicit differentiation
A constant multiple rule
Direct substitution of y=5
items.explanation: Implicit differentiation is especially useful when y is not isolated; the method differentiates the relation directly. It can produce a derivative in terms of both x and y.

items.stem: A student models the cost of fencing a rectangular garden with 100 m of fence, rewrites the cost as one variable, and finds one critical point inside the domain. They conclude that this critical point must give the minimum cost. What should they do next?
options: Check only the critical point.
Compare endpoints and the critical point.
Ignore the domain if a critical point exists.
Use the critical point as the answer immediately.
items.explanation: Closed, bounded optimization problems require checking endpoints as well as critical points. The extrema can occur at an endpoint, so the critical point is not automatically the answer.

items.stem: A student computes \(\int_0^2 x^2\,dx\) and says it is the same type of result as \(\int x^2\,dx\). Which statement is correct?
options: Both are families of functions.
Both are numbers.
The definite integral is a number.
The indefinite integral is a number.
items.explanation: A definite integral evaluates to a number. An indefinite integral represents a family of functions, so the two objects are not the same kind of result.
items.familyKey: a definite integral is the same kind of object as an indefin

items.stem: A teacher asks whether \(\int_0^1 \sqrt{x}\,dx\) can be evaluated even though the function is not negative. A student says only continuous and nonnegative functions can be integrated. What is the best reply?
options: Yes, only continuous and nonnegative functions work.
No, continuity is sufficient but not necessary.
Only nonnegative functions are integrable.
Only continuous functions on \([0,1]\) are integrable.
items.explanation: The definite integral can apply beyond continuous, nonnegative functions. Continuity on a closed interval guarantees integrability, but continuity is sufficient but not necessary.
items.familyKey: only continuous and nonnegative functions can be integrated

items.stem: A student needs \(\int_0^3 (2x+1)\,dx\) and insists it must be found by drawing rectangles or summing Riemann slices. What is the best method?
options: Use FTC Part 2 with an antiderivative.
Use only a geometric area formula.
Riemann sums are the only valid method.
Differentiate the integrand instead.
items.explanation: FTC Part 2 provides a faster method using antiderivatives. Definite integrals do not have to be computed only from areas or Riemann sums.
items.familyKey: definite integrals must always be computed from areas or rie

items.stem: During a run, a student says sweating is a harmful negative effect because it lowers body temperature. Which explanation is best?
options: Negative means harmful, so sweating is bad.
Negative means the response reverses the deviation.
Sweating shuts down homeostasis.
Sweating is not feedback at all.
items.explanation: Negative feedback means the response opposes the deviation to restore the set point. Sweating is a negative-feedback response because it reverses the temperature increase.

items.stem: A student says the stomach is just a larger tissue because it is a single structure. Which correction is most accurate?
options: An organ is one tissue enlarged.
An organ combines two or more tissue types.
A tissue is made of organs.
An organ system is smaller than a tissue.
items.explanation: An organ is not just a bigger tissue. It combines two or more different tissue types into one functional structure, as in the stomach.
items.familyKey: students think an organ is just a bigger version of a tissue

items.stem: A lab uses Gram stain on two unknown bacteria. One stays purple, and the other turns pink after safranin. Which explanation best accounts for the color difference?
options: The stain colors are arbitrary dye choices.
Purple cells have thick peptidoglycan; pink cells have thin peptidoglycan.
Pink cells have thick peptidoglycan; purple cells have thin peptidoglycan.
Both cell types lack peptidoglycan entirely.
items.explanation: The Gram stain reflects real wall structure, not arbitrary dye choice. Thick peptidoglycan retains crystal violet and stays purple, while thin peptidoglycan loses crystal violet and takes up safranin as pink.

items.conceptName: Lipids: saturated, unsaturated, and trans fats
items.stem: A patient says olive oil and trans-fat-rich pastry are both equally harmful because 'all fat is bad.' Which statement is best supported?
options: All dietary fat is harmful in the same way.
Only trans fatty acids raise heart-disease risk; unsaturated fats differ.
Saturated fats are always healthier than unsaturated fats.
Triglycerides are not dietary lipids.
items.explanation: The harmful effect is specific to trans fatty acids and their effect on blood cholesterol. Unsaturated fats such as olive oil behave very differently in the body, so all fat is not bad.
items.familyKey: students treat all dietary fat as harmful all fat is bad

items.stem: A runner starts taking very large doses of vitamin D because 'more is always better.' What is the main concern?
options: Water-soluble vitamins are the only ones stored.
Fat-soluble vitamins can accumulate; excess vitamin D can cause hypercalcemia.
Vitamin D is flushed out immediately in urine.
Megadoses only affect vitamin A, not D.
items.explanation: Fat-soluble vitamins are stored rather than flushed, especially in the liver. Because excess vitamin D can cause hypercalcemia, more is not safer for this class.

items.stem: A student gains weight during a semester and blames only pizza, even though total calories rose from drinks and snacks too. What explains the change best?
options: Pizza uniquely causes fat gain regardless of calories.
Body weight follows total energy balance, not a single food.
Basal metabolism does not affect weight.
Only physical activity determines energy balance.
items.explanation: Body weight tracks the energy ledger: maintained, lost, or gained according to intake versus expenditure. The source of the energy matters less than whether total intake exceeds total expenditure.
items.familyKey: students attribute weight change to specific fattening foods

items.stem: A student says the citric acid cycle is just the next item on a memorized list, so blocking glycolysis would not affect later stages. Which statement best explains what happens in cellular respiration?
options: The stages are arbitrary, so each runs independently.
Blocking glycolysis halts later stages because products feed forward.
Oxidative phosphorylation starts first and powers glycolysis.
The citric acid cycle uses glucose directly, not pyruvate.
items.explanation: Later stages consume the products of earlier ones, so the order is forced by dependency. If glycolysis is blocked, pyruvate is not produced, and the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation stop too.

items.stem: A volcano forms where one oceanic plate sinks beneath another, while another region has plates sliding sideways past each other. What best describes these boundaries?
options: All boundaries are the same kind of collision.
Divergent, convergent, and transform boundaries differ.
Only convergent boundaries create new lithosphere.
Transform boundaries always destroy crust.
items.explanation: There are three distinct types: divergent, convergent, and transform boundaries. They differ in plate motion and what happens to crust, so not all boundaries are collisions.

items.stem: A student claims Andrew Johnson was removed from office after impeachment. What actually happened in 1868?
options: He was removed by the House immediately.
He was acquitted in the Senate by one vote.
He resigned before the Senate trial.
The Supreme Court removed him from office.
items.explanation: He was acquitted in the Senate by one vote short of the required two-thirds majority. In impeachment, the House prosecutes and the Senate decides removal.
items.familyKey: johnson was removed from office after impeachment

items.conceptName: Challenges of rapid urban growth and their roots

options: Urban problems were mainly technical inconveniences.
Urban issues were rooted in class inequality and division.
Cities had no sanitation problems at all.
Only transportation caused urban hardship.

items.conceptName: Farmers’ Alliance to Populist Party (subtreasury plan and Omaha Platform)
items.stem: A farm organization starts with crop loans and warehouse storage, then joins national elections to push railroad regulation and a federal income tax. What shift does this describe?
options: It stayed a self-help group and avoided politics.
It shifted from the Farmers’ Alliance to the Populist Party.
It became a labor union in cities.
It merged with the Republican Party.
items.explanation: The section describes the shift to electoral politics: the alliance formed the Populist Party to enact change through elected representatives. The Omaha Platform extended the subtreasury plan into a broader reform agenda.

items.conceptName: Spanish-American War outcomes and U.S. overseas empire
items.stem: After a quick victory in 1898, U.S. leaders plan for bases in the Pacific and future influence in Asia, not just Cuba. What does this show about their strategy?
options: They focused exclusively on liberating Cuba.
They prepared for the war as empire building.
They intended only defensive coastal protection.
They avoided any overseas expansion.
items.explanation: The passage says strategists prepared for it as a war for empire. Their goals included Pacific bases and expansion toward Asia, not only Cuban liberation.
items.familyKey: u s military strategy focused exclusively on liberating cuba

items.stem: After World War I, a student says Wilson was a pure noninterventionist because he opposed U.S. involvement in other nations’ affairs. Which judgment best fits his foreign policy?
options: He consistently avoided intervention abroad.
He favored restraint, but still intervened when interests were threatened.
He rejected diplomacy and used force immediately.
He ended all overseas markets and ties.
items.explanation: Wilson advocated restraint, but the text says it was hard to keep the U.S. out of world affairs. When American interests were threatened, intervention still followed.

options: War was abolished because it was declared illegal.
The U.S. avoided Europe but kept all global commitments.
The agreements failed because they lacked enforcement action.
The U.S. fully joined European collective security.

A rivalry fought through alliances and propaganda.
A single peace treaty after 1945.
A colonial war over overseas territory.
items.explanation: The Cold War did not include direct military confrontation between Soviet and U.S. troops. It relied on indirect tools like espionage, propaganda, alliances, and an arms race.

One plane crashed in Pennsylvania.
No plane was hijacked successfully.
The fourth plane landed safely.

items.stem: A beginner in Korean tries to translate “Can I get the menu, please?” word for word into Korean and sounds unnatural. What is the best advice?

Memorize common set phrases and polite patterns.
Skip polite endings in restaurants.
Use only banchan names when ordering.
items.explanation: Korean ordering uses fixed polite patterns and different question forms. Learners should memorize common set phrases rather than literal translations.
items.familyKey: students may think they can directly translate english resta

Time also needs counters and time expressions.
Daily routines never use time phrases.
Only days of the week matter in Korean.
items.explanation: Telling time also requires time-related counters and common expressions for hours, minutes, and parts of the day. Numbers alone are not enough to place events accurately.

Skip the title because it is decorative.
Analyze only technical terms immediately.
Search for one correct paraphrase first.
items.explanation: The title is a doorway that sets expectations, and the first pass should orient you to tone, mood, and style. Early reading also notices what stands out or confuses you.

options: It uses in medias res as a deliberate convention.
It is incomplete because the beginning was lost.
The poet ignored earlier events accidentally.
The audience was meant to know no background.

He should remain passive until Odysseus returns.
Parentage is only a biological puzzle.
His identity depends on copying the suitors.

items.conceptName: Austen’s prose style (wit, balance, rhetorical control)
items.stem: A reader says Austen’s prose is too easy to study because her language is “not complex.” Which response best follows the passage?
options: Her balance, sound, and tropes reward close reading.
There is nothing stylistically notable to analyze.
Only plot matters in Austen’s novels.
Her style works only if the sentences are difficult.
items.explanation: The passage argues that Austen’s sentences have balance, sound, and rhetorical tropes worth close reading. Even when the language is not hard, the style reveals social realities beneath polite surfaces.
items.familyKey: if the language is not complex there is little to analyze st

items.stem: A student says a curve is continuous because it can be drawn without lifting the pencil. What is the best correction?
options: That is the formal definition of continuity.
It is only an intuition, not the definition.
It applies only on open intervals.
It ignores left and right limits.
items.explanation: The pencil test is a helpful picture, not the definition. Continuity at a point requires f(a) defined, the limit exists, and the limit equals f(a).
items.familyKey: students treat the graph can be drawn without lifting the pe

items.stem: A function has an interior point c where f'(c) is undefined. What should you conclude when checking for extrema?
options: c cannot matter for extrema.
c is a critical number and possible extremum location.
c must be a local minimum.
c is not in the domain.
items.explanation: An undefined derivative at an interior point still makes c a critical number and a possible extremum location. Critical numbers include points where f'(c) is zero or undefined, so c must be checked.
items.familyKey: if f c is undefined then c cannot matter for extrema

items.stem: A function is bounded on an open interval but is not continuous there. What can you conclude about absolute extrema?
options: It must have both absolute maxima and minima.
Boundedness alone guarantees extrema.
It may fail to have absolute extrema.
It has an absolute maximum only.
items.explanation: Boundedness alone is not enough; continuity on a closed, bounded interval is the key hypothesis in the theorem. An open interval or a discontinuity can prevent absolute extrema from existing.
items.familyKey: if a function is bounded it automatically has absolute maxim

items.stem: A biology lab changes fertilizer amount between two plant groups and then measures plant height after four weeks. Which variable is dependent?
options: Fertilizer amount, because it is the planned change.
Plant height, because it is measured as the outcome.
Both are independent variables.
Neither is a variable in the experiment.
items.explanation: Ask what the researcher changes first; then ask what changes in response. The manipulated fertilizer amount is the independent variable, and plant height is the dependent variable because it is the measured outcome.
items.familyKey: students often swap the independent and dependent variables

items.stem: Which tissue type specializes in rapid communication and signal transmission?
options: Epithelial tissue
Connective tissue
Muscle tissue
Nervous tissue
items.explanation: Nervous tissue contains neurons and supporting cells for communication. The other tissues primarily protect, support, or contract.

items.stem: A biopsy shows cells embedded in abundant extracellular matrix with scattered cells. Which tissue type is most likely?
options: Epithelial tissue
Connective tissue
Muscle tissue
Nervous tissue
items.explanation: Connective tissue is characterized by cells dispersed within an extracellular matrix. This arrangement supports binding, support, and protection.

items.stem: Which tissue type is designed to shorten and generate force for movement?
options: Epithelial tissue
Connective tissue
Muscle tissue
Nervous tissue
items.explanation: Muscle tissue contracts to produce force and movement. Its cells are specialized for contraction rather than lining, support, or signaling.

items.stem: A scientist studies tissue appearance, organization, and function under the microscope. What field is being used?
options: Anatomy
Histology
Physiology
Pathology
items.explanation: Histology focuses on tissues under the microscope, including appearance, organization, and function. It connects structure with what the tissue does.

items.stem: Which structure most directly provides attachment points for skeletal muscles?
options: Bones
Cartilage
Ligaments
Tendons
items.explanation: Bones provide attachment points that muscles pull on during movement. Cartilage cushions, ligaments connect bone to bone, and tendons connect muscle to bone.

items.stem: Which skeletal system function is carried out in bone marrow?
options: Blood cell production
Signal transmission
Hormone secretion
Food digestion
items.explanation: Bone marrow produces blood cells, especially in many flat bones. This is one important internal function of the skeletal system.

items.stem: Which body function is performed by the skeletal system?
options: Pumps blood through vessels
Supports body and enables movement
Produces digestive enzymes
Regulates breathing rate
items.explanation: Bones and cartilage support the body, and bones provide attachment points for muscles to move it. The skeletal system also protects organs and stores minerals, but those are not the best match here.

items.stem: A runner pushes off the ground mainly because bones provide what?
options: Attachment points for muscles
Nerve signals to joints
Stored oxygen for sprinting
Fluid cushions between organs
items.explanation: Bones help movement by serving as attachment points for muscles. When muscles contract, they pull on bones to produce motion.

items.stem: Why is an economic model useful in analyzing consumer choice?
options: It copies every detail of reality exactly.
It keeps relevant features and ignores the rest.
It proves all assumptions are always true.
It replaces data with opinions.
items.explanation: An economic model simplifies reality by keeping features relevant to the question and discarding others. It is useful when its assumptions are close enough for the problem being studied.

items.stem: Which situation is the best example of an externality?
options: A buyer pays a seller for groceries.
A concert increases nearby noise for residents.
A student saves money in a bank account.
A company reports revenue to shareholders.
items.explanation: An externality is a cost or benefit that falls on a third party outside the exchange. Nearby residents experiencing noise from a concert fit that definition.

items.stem: Why might policy correct a pollution externality?
options: To make producers face spillover costs
To eliminate all markets completely
To guarantee higher prices always
To remove consumer preferences
items.explanation: Correcting an externality means making decision-makers face costs the market boundary leaves out. That reduces overproduction caused by prices that ignore spillover harm.

items.stem: If a subsidy encourages bee-keeping because nearby farms benefit from pollination, what is this called?
options: Negative externality
Positive externality
Inflation
Deadweight loss
items.explanation: Pollination creates benefits for third parties who are not part of the bee-keeping transaction. That makes it a positive externality.

items.stem: At a factory, smoke from production harms nearby residents who did not buy the product. What is this called?
options: A negative externality
A public good
A subsidy
A monopoly
items.explanation: The smoke imposes a cost on third parties outside the transaction, so it is a negative externality. Because the market price omits that spillover cost, output tends to be too high relative to the socially efficient level.

items.stem: You want to order politely in Korean and ask for water. What strategy is best?
options: Use a memorized polite set phrase
Translate English word-for-word
Skip polite endings
Use only slang
items.explanation: Korean restaurant speech often relies on fixed polite patterns rather than literal English translation. Memorizing set phrases helps because ordering uses special forms and respect marking.
items.familyKey: students may think they can directly translate english resta

items.stem: Which item is most likely part of a Korean meal served alongside the main dish?
options: Banchan
A tax receipt
A train ticket
A dessert menu
items.explanation: Banchan are side dishes commonly served with Korean meals. They are part of the dining experience and often accompany the main order.

items.stem: At a Korean restaurant, which request is most appropriate?
options: Please bring another side dish
Give me food now
You must hurry
I refuse politeness
items.explanation: A polite request fits Korean restaurant interaction norms. Ordering and asking for items usually uses respectful, set expressions rather than direct commands.

items.stem: Which sentence best fits a morning routine in Korean?
options: 나는 일어나서 아침을 먹습니다.
나는 어제 학교에 갑니다.
나는 책을 오늘 먹습니다.
나는 잠을 점심에 공부합니다.
items.explanation: This sentence sequences routine actions correctly: waking up first, then eating breakfast. Routine descriptions in Korean combine action verbs with time-related sequencing.

items.stem: A student wants to say, “I study after lunch.” Which Korean structure is most appropriate?
options: 점심 후에 공부합니다.
I lunch after study.
공부합니다 점심 후에.
점심은 공부합니다 후에.
items.explanation: 점심 후에 places the time phrase naturally before the verb. Korean routine sentences depend on correct sequencing and time expressions, not English-like word order.

items.stem: What best describes Hangul writing?
options: Letters grouped into stacked syllable blocks.
Words written as separate pictures.
A simple left-to-right alphabet line.
Only consonants are written.
items.explanation: Hangul is alphabetic, but its letters are arranged in stacked syllable blocks. This makes it different from a linear English-style string of letters.
items.familyKey: hangul is an alphabet where letters are written in a simple

items.stem: A beginner wants to read Korean efficiently. What should they learn first?
options: Individual consonants and vowels.
Whole words from a phrasebook.
Only capital letters and punctuation.
Sentence endings before letters.
items.explanation: Learners first master consonants and vowels, then combine them into syllable blocks and words. Memorizing whole words skips the basic structure of Hangul.
items.familyKey: learning hangul means memorizing whole words

items.stem: Which symbol combination is required for a normal Hangul syllable block?
options: At least one consonant and one vowel.
Two vowels and no consonant.
Only one consonant by itself.
Any three English letters.
items.explanation: A Hangul syllable block usually contains at least one consonant and one vowel. That pairing allows the block to be read as a Korean syllable.

items.stem: Why can Hangul letters help learners remember pronunciation?
options: Their shapes often suggest articulation.
They must be memorized as whole words.
They are pronounced only by context.
Their shapes never relate to sound.
items.explanation: The visual shape of a Hangul letter can hint at how it is pronounced or articulated. That makes the writing system useful for connecting form and sound.

items.stem: Which statement best explains when to choose a Korean greeting?
options: Any greeting works in every situation.
Choose based on relationship and politeness.
Use only formal greetings with everyone.
Greetings never change by setting.
items.explanation: Korean greetings depend on relationship, setting, and politeness level. A single expression is not always appropriate across formal, neutral, and casual contexts.
items.familyKey: a single greeting works in every situation

items.stem: A student meets a professor and wants a basic introduction. What should it include?
options: Only their name.
Greeting words, name, and a polite closing.
A long personal story.
No greeting, just silence.
items.explanation: Basic introductions often combine a greeting, the speaker’s name, and a polite closing or self-descriptive phrase. This fits beginner Korean social conventions.
items.familyKey: introductions only require saying a name

items.stem: Which phrase best fits a respectful beginner greeting in Korean?
options: Casual speech to a stranger.
Polite ending with a greeting phrase.
Only a number and name.
A greeting with no context.
items.explanation: Beginner greetings usually use polite sentence endings, especially in respectful situations. They also reflect the relationship and setting.

items.stem: Why might two Korean speakers use different greetings in the same place?
options: Because greetings depend on social context.
Because Korean has no greetings.
Because greetings are random.
Because names replace greetings.
items.explanation: The same location can still involve different relationships and levels of politeness. Korean greetings shift with social context, not just place.

items.stem: Which is the best beginner self-introduction in Korean?
options: Name only, no greeting.
Greeting, name, and polite closing phrase.
Just a bow with no words.
A long explanation of hobbies.
items.explanation: A beginner introduction typically includes greeting words, the person’s name, and a polite closing or short phrase. That matches common introductory patterns.

items.stem: A learner wants to tell someone their age in Korean. What should they do?

Choose the number form for age.
Avoid numbers completely.
Translate the English phrase word-for-word.
items.explanation: Korean uses different number systems in different contexts, including age. Learners must choose the form that fits the grammatical situation.
items.familyKey: one korean number system is used for every counting situatio

items.stem: Which sentence best describes counting nouns in Korean?
options: Nouns are counted without any extra words.
A counter often appears before the noun.
Only native numbers can count nouns.
Counters are used only for ages.
items.explanation: Many Korean nouns require a counter between the numeral and the noun. This is a key part of counting expressions.

items.stem: A student counts three books in Korean. What is the main challenge?
options: Choosing the right counter.
Avoiding all numbers.
Using only one number system.
Leaving out the noun.
items.explanation: Counting objects in Korean often requires selecting the correct counter. The numeral alone is usually not enough for many nouns.

items.stem: Which number system is commonly used for age in many Korean lessons?
options: Native Korean only
Sino-Korean only
Both, depending on context
Neither number system
items.explanation: Korean commonly uses both native Korean and Sino-Korean numbers. Age, quantity, time, and measurement can require different forms and counters depending on context.

items.stem: Which sentence pattern best forms a Korean question?
options: Move the verb to the front.
Keep order, change the ending.
Add a question word only.
Remove the subject entirely.
items.explanation: Korean usually keeps the basic sentence order. A question is marked by the final ending or by a question word in the missing-information spot.

items.stem: Which sentence can be a Korean yes-no question without a question word?

Must every question include 누구?

Questions never use polite forms.

items.stem: Which is the best polite way to ask, “Where are you going?” in Korean?
options: Question word placed where the missing info belongs
Verb moved to the front
No ending change is needed
Only a yes-no ending works
items.explanation: Korean question words can stay in the position of the missing information. Polite question forms are common in beginning communication.

items.stem: A student says they can ask any Korean question by using only rising intonation. What is missing?
options: A special subject marker
A question ending or question word
A past tense marker
A noun counter
items.explanation: Korean questions are not formed by intonation alone. They usually use a final question ending, and wh-questions also use a question word.

items.conceptName: Odyssey vs. Iliad: thematic focus and heroism
items.stem: Which pairing best matches the poems' emphases?
options: Iliad: homecoming; Odyssey: wrath
Iliad: destruction; Odyssey: adaptable intelligence
Iliad: comedy; Odyssey: tragedy
Iliad: peaceful travel; Odyssey: battlefield fury
items.explanation: The Iliad centers on heroic wrath, destruction, and death. The Odyssey centers on adaptability, wisdom, and the return home.

items.conceptName: Odyssey vs. Iliad: thematic focus and heroism
items.stem: Which statement best contrasts the Iliad and the Odyssey?
options: Iliad: homecoming; Odyssey: battlefield wrath.
Iliad: heroic wrath and death; Odyssey: adaptable intelligence.
Iliad: supernatural adventures; Odyssey: historical siege.
Iliad: family restoration; Odyssey: Troy's destruction.
items.explanation: The Iliad centers on wrath, destruction, and death. The Odyssey emphasizes Odysseus’s adaptability, intelligence, and return home to restore family life.

items.stem: After row reduction, which columns are pivot columns?
options: The columns with the largest numerical entries.
The columns containing the first nonzero entry in each row.
The columns with the most zeros.
The last columns in the matrix.
items.explanation: Pivot columns come from pivot positions in echelon form. They are determined by elimination structure, not by entry size.
items.familyKey: the columns with the largest numbers become pivot columns

items.stem: What does row reduction preserve?
options: The solution set of the linear system.
The determinant of every matrix.
The sum of all entries in each row.
The number of columns in the matrix.
items.explanation: Elementary row operations do not change the solution set. They transform the matrix while keeping the same linear system solutions.

items.stem: Why is reduced row echelon form especially useful?
options: It is unique, so different methods reach the same result.
It always makes every entry zero.
It removes all free variables automatically.
It changes the solution set to simplify computation.
items.explanation: Reduced row echelon form is unique, even though the path to it may differ. That makes it a reliable final form for reading solutions.

items.stem: Which operation is linear?
options: Translate every vector by (2,3).
Rotate vectors about the origin.
Move vectors upward by 1.
Shift vectors right by 5.
items.explanation: Rotation about the origin preserves addition and scalar multiplication, so it is linear. Translations change the zero vector and are not linear transformations.

items.stem: Which statement best describes a least-squares regression line?
options: It must pass through all data points.
It minimizes squared vertical errors.
It always has slope 1.
It only works for two points.
items.explanation: The least-squares line minimizes the sum of squared vertical gaps, not the distance to every point. It can miss every data point and still be the best fit.
items.familyKey: a best fit line must pass through the data points

items.stem: When the columns of A are linearly independent, what is true about the least-squares solution?
options: It is unique.
It is impossible to compute.
It equals b exactly.
It must be infinite.
items.explanation: Linearly independent columns make AᵀA invertible, so the least-squares solution is unique. The fitted vector Ax̂ is the projection of b onto the column space of A.

items.stem: Which vector is the least-squares fit to an inconsistent system Ax = b?
options: The x making Ax closest to b.
Any x with Ax = b.
The x with largest entries.
The x that makes residual largest.
items.explanation: Least squares chooses the x that makes Ax as close as possible to b. Equivalently, Ax̂ is the orthogonal projection of b onto the column space of A.

items.stem: Which student behavior best shows semantic encoding of a word list?
options: Repeating the words aloud
Writing each word's meaning
Tracing the word shapes
Listening to the word sounds
items.explanation: Semantic encoding means processing words by meaning, which improves later recall. Merely hearing, saying, or copying the forms is shallower than making meaning-based connections.

items.stem: A teacher wants information to enter memory for later learning. What is the first step?
options: Storage
Retrieval
Encoding
Forgetting
items.explanation: Encoding is the input of information into the memory system. Storage comes after information has been encoded, and retrieval happens when it is later accessed.

items.stem: A student can hold a phone number briefly but loses it after 20 seconds without rehearsal. Which system is involved?
options: Long-term memory
Short-term memory
Procedural memory
Sensory memory only
items.explanation: Short-term memory lasts about 15 to 30 seconds without rehearsal and holds only a limited number of items. Working memory is related, but the brief temporary storage described here is STM.

items.stem: An infant is consistently comforted when distressed. According to Erikson, this supports which conflict?
options: Identity versus role confusion
Trust versus mistrust
Industry versus inferiority
Integrity versus despair
items.explanation: In infancy, Erikson's key task is trust versus mistrust. Reliable comfort helps the child develop trust, which becomes the basis of later development.

items.stem: A retiree reflects on life achievements and regrets. Which Erikson stage is most relevant?
options: Trust versus mistrust
Industry versus inferiority
Identity versus role confusion
Integrity versus despair
items.explanation: Late adulthood involves integrity versus despair, where people evaluate their lives. Erikson saw development as lifelong, so this stage is still psychologically active.

items.stem: Maya keeps painting after class because it feels rewarding. Her art teacher later pays her for each painting. Which change is most likely?
options: Her intrinsic motivation may decrease.
Her intrinsic motivation must increase.
Her extrinsic motivation disappears.
Her interest cannot change over time.
items.explanation: Payment can shift attention from enjoyment to reward, making the activity feel more like work. This overjustification effect often reduces intrinsic motivation, even when the person originally liked the task.

items.stem: Jared studies piano because he loves the music, then starts teaching lessons for money. What is the best description?
options: Only intrinsic motivation is present.
Only extrinsic motivation is present.
Motivation can mix intrinsic and extrinsic factors.
Motivation never changes across situations.
items.explanation: People are usually driven by a mix of intrinsic and extrinsic motives. That mix can shift by context, such as when a hobby becomes partly paid work.
